strengths: Focuses on the relatively underexplored brain encoding direction (predicting neural signals from visual stimuli) rather than the more common brain decoding task.
Evaluates on two benchmark multimodal neuroimaging datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG) across multiple subjects.
Provides extensive topographical visualizations over time windows to inspect spatial and temporal neural dynamics across subjects.
weaknesses: Conceptual disconnect from visual prostheses: The paper frames scalp EEG and MEG generation as brain encoding for visual prostheses. However, clinical visual prostheses (e.g., retinal or intracortical implants) stimulate neural tissue at the cellular or micro-electrode level (such as retinal ganglion cells or V1 columns) to elicit phosphenes. Scalp EEG/MEG field potentials cannot be used directly as stimulation patterns for prostheses, making the central motivational claim biologically and clinically unfounded.

Lack of technical novelty: The proposed architecture simply takes the standard UNet2DConditionModel from Hugging Face Diffusers and conditions it on CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings via standard cross-attention. There is no domain-specific algorithmic contribution or methodological innovation tailored to neural dynamics or signal properties.

Absence of external baselines: The experimental evaluation lacks comparisons to standard neural encoding baselines (e.g., regularized linear/ridge regression, linear-nonlinear Poisson models, CNN-based direct feature-to-EEG regressors, or prior work like Img2EEG). Without comparing against standard deterministic regressors or existing generative models, it is impossible to assess whether a diffusion-based framework provides any tangible benefit.

Incomplete evaluation methodology for generative models: Denoising diffusion models are stochastic generators, yet the paper evaluates them strictly using point-wise Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC). The manuscript does not clarify whether predictions were evaluated on single-trial generations, averaged over multiple stochastic rollouts, or evaluated on distribution-level metrics (e.g., power spectral density matching, frequency-band coherence, or visual concept retrieval/classification accuracy).

Writing and presentation inconsistencies: Informal tone and grammatical slips occur in key sections (e.g., Section 4.4 states 'I have plotted the topography for all subjects...', which is inappropriate for a multi-author technical paper).

strengths: Addresses the challenging task of neural encoding by generating time-resolved neural responses (EEG and MEG) directly from visual images.
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple modalities (THINGS-EEG2 with 10 subjects and THINGS-MEG with 4 subjects), including both within-subject and cross-subject generalization tests.
Extensive qualitative visualizations of scalp topographies across subjects and time windows to inspect spatial activations.
weaknesses: Conceptual disconnect from the stated motivation: The paper heavily frames the work around visual prostheses (retinal/cortical implants). However, visual prostheses require micro-scale spatio-temporal electrical pulse patterns for direct neural stimulation of ganglion cells or cortex. Non-invasive, far-field macro-potentials (scalp EEG/MEG) cannot be directly deployed as stimulation patterns for prostheses, making the clinical/prosthetic motivation largely unsubstantiated.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed architecture is effectively an off-the-shelf 2D U-Net diffusion model (`UNet2DConditionModel` from Hugging Face Diffusers) conditioned on pre-trained CLIP embeddings via standard cross-attention. The model treats the channel-by-time brain matrix as an arbitrary 2D image, ignoring fundamental neurophysiological inductive biases such as 3D sensor geometry, volume conduction, and frequency/phase dynamics.

Complete lack of baseline comparisons: The empirical evaluation does not compare against any existing neural encoding models (e.g., standard linear/ridge regression encoding models, CNN/transformer encoders, Img2EEG by Lu & Golomb, or GAN/VAE-based synthesizers). Without benchmark baselines, it is impossible to determine whether the reported correlation values (PCC ~0.188 for EEG and ~0.122 for MEG) represent competitive or state-of-the-art performance.

Incomplete evaluation of generative signal properties: For time-series and neurophysiological data, standard point metrics like MSE and PCC are insufficient. The paper lacks evaluation on crucial signal characteristics such as power spectral density (PSD), event-related potential (ERP) peak latencies/amplitudes, and single-trial distribution fidelity.

Writing and presentation inconsistencies: In Section 4.4, the narrative abruptly shifts to first-person singular ('I have plotted the topography...'), and the caption for Figure 3 defines the difference topography as training EEG minus test EEG rather than generated versus real signals.

strengths: The paper explores the challenging task of neural encoding, specifically synthesizing high-dimensional time-series electrophysiological responses (EEG and MEG) conditioned on natural visual stimuli.
Experiments are conducted on two large, publicly available datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG), providing both within-subject and cross-subject evaluations.
The manuscript includes extensive qualitative visualizations of topographic response maps across multiple subjects and time intervals in the appendix.
weaknesses: Fundamental disconnect between motivation and methodology: The paper frames itself around visual prostheses (retinal and cortical implants). However, visual prostheses require microscopic stimulation patterns applied directly to retinal ganglion cells or intracortical microelectrodes. Non-invasive, macro-scale scalp EEG (63 channels) and MEG (271 channels) recordings cannot be used as stimulation patterns for visual prosthetics, rendering the central medical/engineering motivation scientifically flawed.

Lack of competitive baselines: The experimental evaluation does not benchmark against any existing neural encoding models, regression baselines (e.g., ridge regression, linear temporal receptive field models), or deep generative models mentioned in related work (e.g., Img2EEG, GAN-based generators). The only comparison provided is an internal ablation over conditioning mechanisms (cross-attention vs. addition/concatenation).

Naive architectural formulation for electrophysiological signals: The framework treats the (Channels × Time) brain signal as a standard 2D image using an off-the-shelf UNet2DConditionModel from Hugging Face. Applying 2D spatial convolutions across arbitrary channel indices ignores the non-Euclidean, 3D sensor geometry of EEG/MEG arrays and fails to capture neurophysiologically meaningful spatial and temporal dynamics.

Inadequate evaluation protocol and low quantitative performance: Given that diffusion models are stochastic generators, the manuscript does not clarify whether the reported PCC and MSE are calculated on single generated trajectories or trial averages. Furthermore, standard evaluation metrics for neural time-series generation (e.g., spectral power fidelity, ERP peak latency/amplitude consistency, or retrieval/classification performance) are omitted. The achieved PCC values (mean ~0.188 on EEG, ~0.122 on MEG) are very low, leaving it unclear whether the model learns meaningful stimulus-specific neural dynamics or merely coarse temporal drifts.

Presentation and writing issues: The writing contains informal and inconsistent phrasings (e.g., the sudden shift to first-person singular 'I have plotted the topography...' on page 7), and the discussion does not critically analyze why the model achieves such low correlation values.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and relatively underexplored direction in cognitive machine learning: neural encoding / generative modeling of continuous non-invasive brain signals (EEG and MEG) conditioned on visual stimuli.

The proposed architecture thoughtfully incorporates domain-specific structure through learnable spatio-temporal position embeddings, which account for anatomical brain regions alongside temporal sequence order.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two established multimodal benchmarks (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG), with ablation studies demonstrating the utility of each component (CLIP text tokens, region embeddings, and temporal embeddings).
The manuscript is clearly structured, easy to read, and provides extensive implementation and configuration details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual mismatch in the clinical/prosthesis framing: The manuscript heavily motivates the work as 'brain encoding for visual prostheses' (predicting stimuli to drive implants). However, visual prostheses stimulate local tissue (e.g., retinal ganglion cells via epiretinal arrays or V1 neurons via intracortical microelectrodes) with specific microcurrent pulse waveforms. Scalp-level M/EEG recordings reflect aggregate postsynaptic potentials across millions of neurons filtered through the skull and scalp; they cannot serve as stimulation parameters for neural implants. The core contribution is actually visual encoding/synthesis of M/EEG, and motivating it as a functional visual prosthesis pipeline is biologically and clinically inaccurate.

Absence of qualitative signal/ERP evaluation in the main text: The paper does not show generated brain signal waveforms, event-related potentials (ERPs), or generated topographies compared against ground truth. Curiously, Figure 3 and Figure 7 merely compare Subject 1's ground truth to Subject 2's ground truth to illustrate inter-subject variability, rather than showing model reconstructions versus ground truth targets.

Relatively weak and sparse baselines: The comparison relies predominantly on classical linear CNN encoding models from a decade ago (Güçlü & Van Gerven, 2015; Yamins et al., 2014) and a single adapted fMRI synthesis method (SynBrain). Stronger contemporary deep neural time-series backbones, conditional continuous diffusion models for 1D/multichannel biosignals, or direct regression transformers (e.g., EEG/MEG foundation backbones) are missing.

Lack of clarity regarding SNR and single-trial vs. trial-averaged evaluation: M/EEG signals have an extremely low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In THINGS-EEG2/MEG, the test split contains multiple repeated presentations (up to 80 for EEG, 12 for MEG). It is unclear whether the model is trained/evaluated on single raw noisy trials or on trial-averaged evoked responses, which significantly impacts the interpretation of metrics like MSE and Pearson correlation.

Severe cross-subject degradation without mitigation: While inter-subject variability is acknowledged, cross-subject correlation plummets to ~0.08–0.15, indicating that the model largely memorizes subject-specific spatio-temporal patterns rather than learning robust image-to-neural representations across individuals.

strengths: Addresses the inverse problem of brain decoding (image-to-brain signal generation / brain encoding) on high temporal-resolution modalities (EEG and MEG), which is less explored than fMRI synthesis.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on two established, large-scale benchmarks: THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG.
Well-structured ablation studies investigating the roles of LLM-generated captions, different LLM backbones, and spatial/temporal positional embeddings.
Neuroscientifically consistent ablation results demonstrating that the removal of occipital electrodes causes the largest degradation in image-driven response prediction.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual mismatch regarding visual prostheses: The paper motivates and frames itself around visual prostheses (in title, abstract, introduction, and Figure 1). However, visual prostheses (e.g., retinal implants or cortical intracortical arrays) require localized electrical microstimulation parameters (e.g., current amplitude, pulse duration, frequency across electrode arrays) to elicit phosphenes. Scalp M/EEG measures macro-level, highly blurred electromagnetic fields outside the skull and cannot serve as electrical stimulation patterns for prosthetic implants. Conflating non-invasive scalp M/EEG encoding with neuroprosthetic stimulus generation undermines the foundational premise of the paper.

Lack of critical evaluation details and noise ceiling analysis: The paper does not clearly specify whether the target brain signals are trial-averaged event-related potentials/fields (ERPs/ERFs) or single-trial recordings. Given that THINGS-EEG2 has 80 repetitions in the test set, single-trial versus trial-averaged evaluation fundamentally changes SNR and performance bounds. Furthermore, the paper omits noise ceiling estimations (e.g., split-half trial consistency), making it impossible to evaluate how close the model is to the explainable variance bound.

Ambiguity in metric definitions: While Appendix F describes Pearson correlation and Cosine similarity conceptually, it does not mathematically define along which dimension(s) they are computed (e.g., computed per channel across time and averaged, per time-point across channels, or flattened across the entire channel-time matrix).

Limited and dated baselines: The comparison models consist of two classical linear encoding models from 2014 and 2015 (Güçlü & Van Gerven; Yamins et al.) and one adapted fMRI framework (SynBrain). The benchmark lacks modern deep learning architectures or contemporary diffusion/generative models adapted for time-series and M/EEG data.

Limited technical novelty: The technical components—a standard Diffusion Transformer (DiT), cross-attention conditioning on concatenated CLIP image/text embeddings, and additive spatio-temporal positional embeddings—are standard combinations of off-the-shelf generative modeling techniques with minimal domain-specific architectural innovation.

Cross-subject collapse without methodological solutions: When evaluated across subjects, performance drops drastically (e.g., Pearson r drops from 0.425 to 0.157 on EEG, and from 0.379 to 0.082 on MEG). While the authors acknowledge subject variability, no adaptation, alignment, or subject-conditioning mechanisms are introduced to mitigate this limitation.

strengths: The paper addresses the challenging problem of neural encoding (synthesizing M/EEG responses from visual inputs), which is less explored than visual decoding from brain signals.
The architecture systematically integrates visual and semantic representations by combining CLIP image embeddings with LLM-generated captions as conditions for a Diffusion Transformer (DiT).
Experiments are conducted on two large-scale public multimodal datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG), evaluating both within-subject and cross-subject performance.
The manuscript is clearly written, well-organized, and provides pseudocode and configuration details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Conceptual disconnect regarding visual prostheses: The paper motivates the task as the 'brain encoding stage of visual prostheses' to predict stimulation patterns for retinal or cortical implants. However, scalp M/EEG signals are blurred, macro-level electrophysiological recordings outside the skull and are not used as electrode stimulation protocols in visual prostheses (which require micro-scale current/voltage pulses delivered directly to retinal ganglion cells or V1 neurons). Framing macro-scale M/EEG synthesis as a functional component of visual prostheses is biologically and clinically unfounded.

Absence of qualitative signal and topography visualizations: The paper never displays the generated M/EEG signals or their reconstructed topographies alongside the ground truth. Figures 3 and 7 only plot ground-truth data from Subject 1 vs. Subject 2 to illustrate inter-subject variability, but fail to show whether the model actually captures event-related potentials (ERPs/ERFs, such as the P100 or N170) or realistic temporal dynamics.

Outdated and limited baselines: The comparison models are predominantly early linear regression models on CNN features (Güçlü & van Gerven, 2015; Yamins et al., 2014) from a decade ago, alongside an adaptation of an fMRI synthesis method (SynBrain). Stronger contemporary neural time-series generation baselines, conditional 1D/2D diffusion models, or modern deep encoding architectures are missing.

Evaluation protocol and missing variance metrics: EEG and MEG data are inherently noisy and trial-variable. The paper does not specify whether evaluation is performed on single trials or trial-averaged ERPs, nor does it report standard deviations across subjects or runs in Tables 1–6, making it difficult to assess statistical significance.

Methodological novelty is limited: The proposed framework is essentially a direct combination of existing building blocks (DiT, DDIM, CLIP vision/text encoders, LLM captioning, and standard 1D/2D additive spatio-temporal position encodings) applied to concatenated channel-time matrices without domain-specific innovations.
